chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid and a group of my scholars narrated to me from Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from al-Husayn ibn Abi Ghundar, from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I heard him say regarding the owl: He said, 'Has any one of you seen it during the day?' They said to him, 'It hardly appears during the day, and it does not appear except at night.' He said: 'Indeed, it has always taken developed structures as abodes. But when al-Husayn (peace be upon him) was killed, it vowed upon itself that it would not take developed structures as abodes ever again, and it would not take anything but wreckages as abodes. So it remains fasting and grieving during its day until night covers it. And when night covers it, it does not cease chanting in grief over al-Husayn (peace be upon him) until morning.'

key_terms.تَرِنُّ: Chanting / lamenting with a specific tone

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the owl's behavior in Shia tradition regarding Imam al-Husayn?
ai.summary: In *Kamil al-Ziyarat*, Ibn Qulawayh records this tradition to highlight the cosmic resonance of Imam al-Husayn’s martyrdom, where the owl’s behavioral shift from day to night symbolizes the transition from the tranquility of the pre-Shahada era to the enduring grief of the Ummah. This narrative underscores the Shia concept of *al-Gha’bah* (the hidden sorrow) manifesting in nature, reinforcing the spiritual significance of night-time lamentations and the owl as a perpetual witness to the Ahl al-Bayt’s suffering.
